### Alternative models without epistasis

To understand the effects of specific epistasis on protein function and evolution, we compared the third-order model described above to models that do not incorporate any epistasis, and thus contain only first-order terms (first-order model), or no higher order epistasis, and thus contains only first- and second-order terms (second-order model). To implement these lower order models, we modified the matrix of indicator variables by removing all indicators for combinations at the orders to be excluded. These models were then fit to the data using analogous selection procedures for the full model containing first-, second-, and third-order terms.

### Comparison to observed DMS data

To estimate the quality of the model fit, we compared the observed class of each protein variant to the observed classification from the empirical data. In each case, we calculated the number of true positives, true negatives, false positives, and false positives for each of the three activation categories, as well as a ‘non-strong’ category (union of null and weak) and an ‘activators’ category (union of weak and strong) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).

### Comparison to measured ΔG

We compared the estimated genetic score for a subset of protein variants to their energy of binding to ERE and SRE, previously measured using fluorescence anisotropy (Anderson et al., 2015; Figure 1—figure supplement 4). We used simple least-squares linear regression to estimate the relationship between the genetic score and the ΔG of binding. Because both genetic score and ΔG accrue additively, the relationship between these quantities should be linear. The slope and intercept of the relationship between genetic score and ΔG was then used it to estimate the ΔG of binding for all variants in the data set from their genetic score.

### Model variance explained by individual terms

The reference-free coding of model coefficients leads to a simple relationship between the effect size of a term and the fraction of genetic variance in phenotype that it explains. A detailed proof is provided in Appendix 1 and summarized here.

The genetic variance is defined as the variance in phenotype attributable to all the effects of individual genetic states and combinations; it excludes genetic variance caused by nonspecific epistasis (which is captured by the logit function in our model). The total genetic variance is the average squared deviation of each variant’s genetic score from the global mean:

$$
Var(y(G))=\frac{1}{2⋅20^{4}}\sumg\inG(y(g)−y(G)¯)^{2}
$$

where $G$ is the set of all protein variants on either RE, y(g) is the genetic score of a particular protein-RE complex, and 2 x 204 is the total number of complexes.

The total variance explained by a model can be partitioned into the partial variances explained by each causal factor. In the case of our model, the total genetic variance can be partitioned into the partial variances attributable to the possible states at each site or (combination of states at multiple sites). Organizing these partial variances by the epistatic order and effect type (nonspecific or RE-specific):

$$
Var(y(G))=\sumiVar(\beta_{i})+\sumi<jVar(\beta_{i,j})+\sumi<j<kVar(\beta_{i,j,k})+Var(\sigma_{0})+\sumiVar(\sigma_{i})+\sumi<jVar(\sigma_{i,j})+\sumi<j<kVar(\sigma_{i,j,k})
$$

where i, j, and k index the four variable sites, the variances are over all the possible states (or combinations), and the summations are over all sites (or combination).

The model coefficients have a straightforward relationship to this partitioned variance. Main-effect coefficients are defined as the average deviation of a subset of variants containing a state or combination relative to the global mean, and higher-order coefficients are defined as deviations from the sum of lower-order terms. The variance attributable to any state (or combination) is therefore simply the square of its coefficients, and the variance attributable to any set of states is the average of the squared coefficients (see proof in Appendix 1). Thus, for any given site i (or site combination i,j or i,j,k), the variance attributable to the set of model terms applicable to that site can be written as follows:

$$
Var(\beta_{i})=\frac{1}{20}\sumq\beta_{q_{i}}^{2}Var(\beta_{i,j})=\frac{1}{20^{2}}\sumq^{2}\beta_{q_{i}q_{j}}^{2}Var(\beta_{i,j,k})=\frac{1}{20^{3}}\sumq^{3}\beta_{q_{i}q_{j}q_{k}}^{2}Var(\sigma_{0})=\sigma_{0}^{2}Var(\sigma_{i})=\frac{1}{20}\sumq\sigma_{q_{i}}^{2}Var(\sigma_{i,j})=\frac{1}{20^{2}}\sumq^{2}\sigma_{q_{i}q_{j}}^{2}Var(\sigma_{i,j,k})=\frac{1}{20^{3}}\sumq^{3}\sigma_{q_{i}q_{j}q_{k}}^{2}
$$

The leading factors in Equation 2 can all be expressed as a function of O, the epistatic order of the effect they represent, where O=0 for the global average effect of the RE, and 1, 2, or 3 for the main, pairwise, and third-order epistatic effects of each amino acid combination. Substituting into Equation 1, the total genetic variance is therefore the sum of the squared effects of every model term at every order (except for the global average), each divided by the number of model terms at that order:

$$
Var(y(G))=\sum\beta,O\neq0\frac{\beta^{2}}{20^{O(\beta)}}+\sum\sigma\frac{\sigma^{2}}{20^{O(\sigma)}}
$$

We can use this same approach to calculate $FVar\theta$ , the fraction of the total genetic variance explained by any coefficient $\theta$ (a particular $\beta$ or $\sigma$ of any order, except the global average):

$$
FVar\theta=\frac{\frac{\theta^{2}}{20^{O\theta}}}{VaryG}
$$

The fraction of genetic variance explained by any set of coefficients is simply the sum of $FVar\theta$ over all the coefficients in the set.

This formalizes the intuition that within an epistatic order, model terms of large magnitude explain more variation than smaller terms; if two terms at different order have the same magnitude, the lower order term explains more variation than the higher-order term, because the former affects more genotypes than the latter. The leading terms effectively weight each set of coefficients in a set by the number of genotypes to which they apply.

We used this simple relationship between the magnitude of a model coefficient, its order of epistatic effect, and the fraction of genetic variance explained by that coefficient to directly calculate the percent of variance explained by every model term. We then summed the percent variance explained by individual terms to determine the percent of variance explained by sets of terms (Figure 2). Finally, we used this relationship to define the ‘important’ terms in the model as those terms needed to explain 99% of the model variance. Thus setting all of the ‘unimportant’ terms to zero reduces the amount of variance explained by less than 1% of the full model (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).

### Fraction of genetic score attributable to epistasis or specificity

To find the relative impact of epistasis terms on each variant’s genetic score, we calculated the sum of the absolute value of all pairwise and third-order model terms for that genotype and divided it by the sum of the absolute value of all model terms for that genotype (Figure 3; Figure 3—figure supplement 1; Figure 3—figure supplement 2). For specificity, we summed the absolute value of only the specificity terms divided by the total absolute sum of all terms.

### Types of epistasis

Epistasis can be divided into several subtypes depending on the signs and magnitude of mutational effects on different genetic backgrounds. These distinctions are most commonly made for pairwise epistatic interactions. For example, sign epistasis arises when the direction of effect of a mutation depends on the genetic background. Reciprocal sign epistasis occurs when the direction of effect of both mutations depends on the genetic background. All other instances of epistasis are classified as magnitude epistasis. Within magnitude epistasis, there are two broad forms, diminishing returns and diminishing costs epistasis. The former, diminishing returns, also includes common forms of epistasis such as amplifying costs, differing only on which genotype is considered ‘wild-type’ or the starting point of a mutant cycle. Likewise, diminishing costs epistasis also covers amplifying returns epistasis, only differing in which genotype is considered the beginning of a mutant cycle.

To classify the types and frequencies of different forms of epistasis, we compared the estimated effect of each pairwise interaction to the estimated effect of each single amino acid involved in that pairwise interaction. The fraction of genetic variance explained by the particular pairwise effect was then added to the appropriate category, either sign, reciprocal sign, diminishing returns, or diminishing costs epistasis. To extend this approach to third-order interactions, we sequentially fixed each amino acid in the third order interaction, taking that genotype as the starting genotype and then varied the other two amino acids in a manner analogous to the pairwise epistasis calculation. The fraction of genetic variance explained by a particular third order interaction was then divided by three (as there are three states that can be fixed) and added to the appropriate category (Figure 3; Figure 3—figure supplement 4).

### Direction of the effect of mutations’ effects

The genetic score of a specific genotype is the summation of the effects in that sequence, that is the single global term, four single site effects, six pairwise interactions, and four three-way interactions for both binding and specificity. The model thus gives the effect of each amino acid or interaction relative to the average of all genotypes, not the effect of individual mutations from one state to another. To calculate the effect of a mutation in a given genetic background, we calculated the difference in the genetic score between two genotypes with a single amino acid difference. This entails a change in one main effect, three pairwise interactions, and three third-order interactions. In this way, the model directly captures the fact that even a single amino acid change has the potential to alter numerous epistatic interactions. As a result, to determine the effect of a mutation requires measuring its impact across numerous genetic backgrounds. To determine the range of possible effects of a single mutation, we compared the genetic score between two genotypes differing by a single amino acid on each of the 8000 genetic backgrounds on which the particular change from one amino acid to another could occur and determined the frequency in which that particular mutation increased or decreased binding on a particular DNA element. To minimize the effect of small changes in genetic score upon mutation being counted, we only considered changes in genetic score greater than 5% of the difference between the average genotype and the threshold needed to be classified as a strong activator. We also used the fact that the model identifies which epistatic factors (main, pairwise, third-order) are responsible for the change in genetic score between variants, as well as how this effect is partitioned between binding and specificity, to identify when changes in epistasis were necessary, sufficient, or both for the change in genetic score (Figure 4; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).

### Sequence space analysis

#### Network types

To determine how epistasis affected the evolution of DBD binding specificity, we generated connected networks for each model of epistasis using the R package igraph (Csárdi and Nepusz, 2006). In each case, genotypes were connected if they differed by a single amino acid (hamming distance) or if the single amino acid difference could occur via a single nucleotide mutation (genetic code distance). In the latter case, we accounted for the disjoint nature of serine codons in the genetic code, treating the two groups as non-interchangeable by coding all serine amino acids in both an S and a Z form. Thus, for a sequence containing n serine amino acid, there are 2n versions of that amino acid sequence with the same phenotype that inhabit different locations in sequence space with different connectivity to neighboring sequences. We created networks for the full model, the model containing up to pairwise epistasis, and the model containing no specific epistasis (Figure 5; Figure 5—figure supplement 1). We used only those genotypes that were functional in a particular model, that is were either weak or strong on either ERE, SRE, or both. In addition, we created a network of all 160,000 genotypes. This latter network contained no information about the function of each genotype and was used to model evolution over sequence space unconstrained by function.

#### Network distance

Network distances were calculated as the shortest path distance between two genotypes, constrained to only take steps to neighboring genotypes in a network. Because only functional genotypes are present in a network, the distance between genotypes in a network can exceed four, even when connections are made by hamming distance, if there are no direct paths between the genotypes. We also calculated the distance from each ERE-specific genotype to the nearest SRE-specific genotype, of which there may be several, by finding the minimum distance for each ERE-specific genotype (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).

#### Shared vs unique network genotypes

One of the main effects of epistasis is to influence whether a genotype is functional or not. Thus, many genotypes are only functional in one or a subset of networks. However, even if the same genotypes are functional with and without epistasis, epistasis can influence the paths between them that evolution is likely to take. To distinguish between these effects, we compared the effects of epistasis on path lengths for all functional genotypes and for the set of genotypes that are functional in all three networks.

#### One-step functional transitions and epistatic necessity/sufficiency

To determine how epistasis influenced changing binding classes or specificity, we identified all instances in which two neighboring genotypes in a network differ in binding class or specificity. These represent portions of sequence space where a single amino acid mutation can move a genotype from one binding class to another or alter specificity from ERE-specific to SRE-specific. For changes between binding classes, we identified all such mutations on the full network with third order epistasis. For changes in specificity, we identified the mutation responsible for all such instances in the full network, as well as the networks that had no third-order epistasis or had no epistatic effects (Figure 4; Figure 4—figure supplement 2).

We calculated whether epistasis was necessary, sufficient, or both for transitions in binding classes and specificity. For binding classes, epistasis was categorized as necessary if the main effect of the amino acid change was not large enough to move the genotype into the new binding class without contribution from the epistatic effects. Similarly, epistasis was categorized as sufficient if epistatic changes were large enough to move the genotype into the new binding class without contribution from the main effects. For single step transitions in specificity, epistasis was necessary if the main, non-epistatic, effect of an amino acid change was not large enough to either reduce ERE binding or increase SRE binding enough to switch the binding class from ERE-specific to SRE-specific. Epistasis was sufficient if the epistatic effects alone were large enough to both reduce ERE binding and increase SRE binding enough to switch the binding class from ERE-specific to SRE-specific. In the full model, a similar distinction was made for third order epistasis relative to main effects and pairwise epistasis and calculated in an analogous manner.

#### Number of paths and path distinctiveness

The number of paths between two genotypes was calculated as the number of distinct shortest paths between them. Two paths were considered distinct if at least one genotype along the paths were different. To account for the fact that many paths traverse similar sets of genotypes, we also developed a metric for distinctiveness of a set of paths between two genotypes. To calculate this metric, we extracted from the larger network the set of genotypes along any shortest path between the starting and ending genotype. Intuitively, for a path with S genotypes, the set of paths between the starting and ending genotypes should be considered more distinct if they contain more unique genotypes or fewer shared edges between intermediate genotypes. To capture these aspects, we calculated two metrics. The first metric relates the effective number of paths (Pg) to the number of unique genotypes (G) and the path length (S - 1). The second metric relates a different measure of the effective number of paths (Pe) to the number of unique edges (E) and the number of genotypes along a single path (S).

$$
P_{g}=\frac{G−2}{S−1}andP_{e}=\frac{E}{S}
$$

The first calculation provides the maximum number of completely distinct paths with no shared genotypes that could be created given the path length and the number of genotypes present. It thus provides an upper bound on the number of distinct paths possible. If a set of paths are completely distinct, that is sharing no genotypes, then Pg will equal Pe. However, if the paths are not completely distinct, then there will be more edges among the set of paths than if all paths were distinct. Thus, for a given number of genotypes and path length, the greater the number of edges connecting those genotypes, the less distinct the set of paths are. By comparing the difference in these metrics to the maximum possible value, we can estimate the effective number of distinct paths (D) in a set.

$$
D=P_{g}−(P_{e}−P_{g})\frac{P_{g}}{P_{e}}=\frac{P_{g}^{2}}{P_{e}}=\frac{S(\frac{G−2}{S−1})^{2}}{E}
$$

We used this equation to calculate the distinctiveness of paths from each ERE-specific genotype to each SRE-specific genotype over the network.

### Evolutionary simulations

#### Neutral model

To determine whether epistasis increased or decreased the ability of evolution to find a protein variant with altered specificity, we performed forward evolutionary simulations over the previously described genotype networks. These simulations captured neutral wandering among a set of functional variants and are similar to the verbal model of protein evolution described by Smith, 1969. In each simulation, evolution was constrained to move among only functional variants, that is those classified by the particular model as either ERE-specific, SRE-specific or promiscuous. Genotypes were classified as either ERE-specific if they bound ERE and not SRE, SRE-specific if they bound SRE and not ERE, and promiscuous if they bound both ERE and SRE. Genotypes were considered neighbors if a single nucleotide change could mutate one variant into the other (genetic code) or if they differed by a single amino acid (hamming distance). To estimate the global effect of epistasis, evolution was initiated from each ERE-specific genotype and allowed to take a random step to a neighboring genotype, regardless of DNA binding specificity, until an SRE-specific genotype was reached. This was repeated 100 times for each starting genotype. For the subset of ERE-specific genotypes found in each of the three models with varying amounts of epistasis (Full model, pairwise only, no epistasis), an additional 1000 simulations were performed to estimate how epistasis altered particular evolutionary paths. For each simulation, we recorded the number of steps, ending genotype identity, and the identity of each intermediate genotype during the evolutionary walk.

#### Model with selection for increased specificity

To estimate how epistasis might interact with selection for increased specificity, we performed additional forward evolutionary simulations. As before, evolution was initiated from ERE-specific genotypes and terminated when an SRE-specific genotype was first encountered. Unlike the neutral simulations, however, we incorporated selection for increased specificity. At each step, the specificity of each neighboring genotype was calculated from the underlying genetic scores as the difference in binding to SRE and ERE. We then used Kimura’s formula for fixation probability to calculate the relative probability of fixation among all possible neighbors (Kimura, 1962). The effects of specificity were scaled such that the difference between a non-binder and a strong binder corresponded to a scaled selection coefficient (i.e. Ns) of 1 in a population of size 100. We initiated evolution with a range of population sizes between 1 and 10,000 to capture the transition between neutrality and selection driven changes, performing 100 simulations for each population size on each network using the genetic code to connect genotypes. We noticed during these simulations, that for a small subset of starting genotypes, evolution would often become ‘stuck’ on local optimum in the pairwise model, continuously cycling between two genotypes. These genotypes were substantially more SRE-specific than the neighboring functional sequences. Simulations with strong selection for specificity (i.e. large population sizes) were therefore more likely to continuously cycle between these genotypes. To account for this effect, we also estimated evolutionary path lengths after removing all evolutionary simulations in which more than 20 steps were taken (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.88737.3.sa1](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.88737.3.sa1)

Metzger et al develop a rigorous method filling an important unmet need in protein evolution - analysis of protein genetic architecture and evolution using data from combinatorially complete 20^N variant libraries. Addressing this need has become increasingly valuable, as experimental methods for generating these datasets expand in scope and scale. Their method integrates two key features - (1) it reports the effects of mutations relative to the average across all variants, rather than a particular genotype, making it useful for examining global genetic architecture, and (2) it does this for all possible 20 states at each site, in contrast to the binary analyses in prior work. These features are not individually novel but integrating them into a single analysis framework is novel and will be valuable to the protein evolution community. Using a previously published dataset generated by two of the authors, they conclude that (1) changes in function are largely attributable to pairwise but not higher-order interactions, and (2) epistasis potentiates, rather than constrains, evolutionary paths. These findings are well-supported by the data. Overall, this work has important implications for predicting the relationship between genotype and phenotype, which is of considerable interest to protein biochemistry, evolutionary biology, and numerous other fields.

results.result: The study analyzed a complete combinatorial library of 160,000 protein variants at four sites in the recognition helix using a FACS-based Sort-seq assay in yeast. Categorization of variants into activation classes substantially reduced technical noise, achieving >97% concordance between replicates, and identified 1342 strong and 3166 weak activators across both response elements.
results.evaluation: Claims C26-C30 describe the experimental design and data quality. The library design (C26), experimental methodology (C27), and data quality metrics (C28-C30) are clearly documented with quantitative measures. The high concordance between replicates (>97%) and the number of variants in each class provide strong evidence for the reliability of the experimental data.

results.result: An ordinal logistic regression model was developed to dissect genetic architecture, incorporating main effects and epistatic effects up to third order. The model achieved excellent fit to experimental data (99.5% correct classification, deviance 0.86) and genetic scores correlated well with independently measured binding energies (R²=0.75).
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C35 describe the model structure and validation. The model's predictive accuracy (C33), goodness-of-fit (C34), and correlation with independent measurements (C35) provide strong evidence that the model captures the genetic architecture effectively. The validation against independent binding measurements is particularly important for establishing model validity.

results.result: The genetic architecture of DNA recognition is dominated by main effects and pairwise epistasis, with higher-order epistasis playing only a minor role. Main effects account for more than half of genetic variance and primarily determine nonspecific binding, while pairwise interactions explain the majority of RE-specificity. Third-order epistasis accounts for only 2% of total variance. The architecture is dense at low orders, with the 99% variance set including all main effects and >80% of pairwise terms but only 5% of third-order terms.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C5 and C36-C43 present the core findings on genetic architecture. The variance decomposition analysis provides quantitative support for the dominance of low-order effects. The density of the architecture at first and second orders (C41-C43) is well-documented. However, the claim that higher-order epistasis is unimportant should be interpreted cautiously, as the study only examined up to third-order effects and used an ordinal model that may have reduced precision.

results.result: Structural rationalization of sequence-function relationships shows that small-volume amino acids at site 2 combined with basic residues at site 3 favor nonspecific binding, while small hydrophobic residues at site 4 favor SRE binding by packing against SRE-specific methyl groups.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C45 provide structural interpretation of the genetic architecture. These interpretations are consistent with known protein-DNA interaction principles and the structural data referenced (Figure 2J). However, these are post-hoc rationalizations rather than predictions, and alternative structural explanations may exist.

results.result: Epistatic interactions overwhelmingly enhance rather than impair protein function, contrary to the 'diminishing returns' expectation. Epistatic terms make net positive contributions to 100% of strong activators and 98% of weak activators, contributing an average of 64% of the score needed for strong activation. Removing epistasis reduces the number of strong activators by ~25% and changes which sequences are functional.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C52 demonstrate that epistasis enhances function. The quantitative data (C47-C51) strongly support this conclusion. The comparison between models with and without epistasis (C50-C51) provides direct evidence for epistasis's functional importance. The finding that states with positive main effects have positive epistatic interactions (C52) provides mechanistic insight. This is a major finding that challenges prevailing views about epistasis.

results.result: There are >200,000 context-specific mutations that can transform null proteins into functional activators, involving 1160 different mutation types. In 99% of cases, epistatic effects are positive, in 94% epistasis is necessary for functional transitions, and in almost half it is sufficient. Sign epistasis is pervasive, with every mutation type showing positive effects in some backgrounds and negative effects in others.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C59 characterize the mutational landscape. The large number of functional transitions (C53-C54) and the quantitative analysis of epistatic contributions (C55-C57) are well-supported by the model. The finding of universal sign epistasis (C58-C59) is particularly striking. These results depend on the model's accuracy, which has been validated, but the biological significance of mutations with small effects should be interpreted cautiously.

results.result: Hundreds of single-residue mutations can switch specificity from ERE to SRE, and epistasis is critical for these transitions. In every case, epistatic effects are necessary for specificity switching, and in almost half they are sufficient. Without epistasis, the number of specificity-switching mutations is reduced by >80%.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C63 demonstrate epistasis's role in functional evolution. The quantitative data on specificity-switching mutations (C60, C63) and the necessity/sufficiency analysis (C61-C62) provide strong evidence. The comparison to the no-epistasis model (C63) directly demonstrates epistasis's importance. This is a key finding for understanding how new functions evolve.

results.result: Despite pervasive sign epistasis, 99.8% of functional sequences are connected in a single mutually accessible network. Epistasis enlarges the network (1603 vs 1080 functional nodes), shortens evolutionary paths to new functions (average 25% reduction in path length, 10% shorter minimum distance), increases the number of single-step transitions between functions (2.5-fold more SRE-specific neighbors per ERE-specific node), and increases the number and diversity of evolutionary paths (average 65 paths per node, 20% more than without epistasis).
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C70 demonstrate that epistasis facilitates rather than constrains evolution. The network analysis provides multiple quantitative measures showing epistasis's facilitating effects. The evolutionary simulations (C66) and network metrics (C67-C70) converge on the same conclusion. However, these analyses assume that all functional variants are equally accessible evolutionarily, which may not reflect biological reality where fitness differences matter.

results.result: The historical ancestral sequences (egKa and GSKV) are only functional because of pairwise epistasis; they would be non-functional under a main-effects-only model. The evolutionary transition from ERE- to SRE-specificity altered the genetic architecture itself, changing which sites and pairs determine function. The final substitution replaced the initial determinants of SRE specificity with a different set of interactions, resulting in a final sequence with entirely different functional determinants than the ancestral sequence.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C76 apply the model to historical evolution. The finding that ancestral sequences require epistasis for function (C71-C73) is well-supported by the model. The observation that genetic architecture changed during evolution (C74-C76) is a novel insight. However, these conclusions depend on the accuracy of ancestral sequence reconstruction and the assumption that the model accurately captures historical genetic architecture.

results.result: The study's findings differ from prior work because it takes a global rather than local view of epistasis and analyzes all 20 amino acid states. Unlike most previous studies, this work found only a small role for higher-order epistasis and a dense rather than sparse genetic architecture. These differences likely arise because prior work used reference-based methods and/or did not adequately account for global nonlinearities.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C82 explain differences from prior work. The methodological differences (C77, C80) are clearly documented. The comparison to prior findings (C79, C81) is supported by citations. The proposed explanations for differences (C80, C82) are plausible but somewhat speculative. The authors appropriately acknowledge that analyzing all 20 states rather than just two may contribute to the observed density.

results.result: Prior work viewed epistasis as an evolutionary constraint by focusing on direct paths between designated sequences in binary sequence space. This study shows that epistasis primarily facilitates functional evolution by expanding the network of functional sequences and bringing variants with different functions closer together in sequence space, making the topography idiosyncratic enough for new functions to be accessible but not so idiosyncratic that functional nodes become isolated.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C86 present the study's main conceptual contribution. The characterization of prior work (C84-C85) is accurate and well-cited. The facilitating role of epistasis (C83, C86) is supported by the network and evolutionary simulation results. However, the conclusion that epistasis facilitates evolution depends on the specific evolutionary scenarios modeled and may not generalize to all contexts.

results.result: The study has several limitations: the ordinal model may reduce precision compared to continuous data analysis, though it reduces noise impact; only four sites in one protein were studied, limiting generalizability; and results may not extrapolate to complex organismal phenotypes. However, the finding that higher-order epistasis is relatively unimportant suggests that modeling first- and second-order terms may be sufficient for most genetic variation in protein functions.
results.evaluation: Claims C87-C93 acknowledge limitations and implications. The authors appropriately recognize methodological limitations (C87-C88) and scope limitations (C89, C92-C93). The suggestion that prior work on other proteins supports dense architecture (C90) is well-cited. The implication for future work (C91) is reasonable but should be tested empirically. The acknowledgment that results may not generalize to complex phenotypes (C92-C93) is important and appropriate.

results.result: Prior research has proposed that protein genetic architecture is complex with pervasive epistatic interactions that constrain evolution. Most prior work has analyzed only direct paths between two proteins, assessed just two states per site, used reference-based methods, and focused on single functions, thus excluding most potential genotypes and evolutionary trajectories.
results.evaluation: Claims C2-C3 and C10-C17 characterize prior work in the field. These characterizations are well-supported by extensive citations. The authors accurately identify limitations in prior approaches, including the focus on binary sequence spaces (C15), reference-based methods (C17), and limited consideration of functional specificity. This provides important context for understanding the novelty of the current study.

results.result: Steroid hormone receptors are ligand-activated transcription factors with two major subfamilies recognizing distinct DNA response elements: ERs bind ERE (AGGTCA) and kSRs prefer SRE (AGAACA). The reconstructed ancestral proteins AncSR1 and AncSR2 were ERE-specific and SRE-specific, respectively, and three substitutions in the recognition helix during the interval between them caused the evolutionary change in specificity.
results.evaluation: Claims C18-C25 provide biological background. The characterization of steroid hormone receptors (C18-C21) represents established knowledge supported by citations. The findings about ancestral proteins (C22-C25) are from prior experimental work by the same research group, providing a solid foundation for the current study. This background is essential for understanding the biological significance of the results.

results.result: The genetic architecture of DNA recognition in the steroid hormone receptor consists primarily of main effects and pairwise epistasis, with higher-order epistasis playing only a minimal role. Main effects account for more than half of genetic variance, pairwise interactions explain the majority of RE-specificity, and third-order epistasis accounts for only 2% of total variance.
results.evaluation: All three reviewers explicitly affirm this finding. The editor states 'changes in function are largely attributable to pairwise rather than higher-order interactions,' and reviewers describe the findings as 'well-supported by the data' and 'convincing.' No concerns are raised about these core architectural findings.

results.result: Pairwise interactions enlarge the set of functional sequences and are the primary determinants of specificity for different DNA elements, while main effects primarily determine nonspecific DNA binding.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these findings without challenge. One reviewer notes the study provides 'convincing results to support the importance of epistasis in promoting evolution of protein functions,' which encompasses these specificity claims. The functional role of pairwise interactions is treated as a well-supported conclusion.

results.result: Epistasis facilitates rather than constrains evolution by enhancing function of active variants, massively expanding opportunities for specificity-switching mutations, and bringing variants with different functions close together in sequence space. Epistatic terms make net positive contributions to 100% of strong activators and 98% of weak activators, contrary to expectations of diminishing returns.
results.evaluation: This is identified as a fundamental finding by all reviewers. The editor states 'epistasis potentiates rather than constrains evolutionary paths' as a key conclusion, and reviewers describe the evidence as 'compelling' and 'convincing.' One reviewer explicitly notes 'This conclusion is impactful because many previous studies have shown that epistasis constrains evolution.'

results.result: There are >200,000 context-mutations that can transform null proteins into functional activators, with epistasis being critical to these transitions. Sign epistasis is rampant, with every mutation type showing positive effects in some backgrounds and negative effects in others, yet in 99% of cases the net epistatic impact is positive and in 94% of cases epistasis is necessary for functional promotion.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these findings as part of the well-supported evidence for epistasis facilitating evolution. The quantitative results on context-dependent mutations are not questioned, and reviewers describe the analyses as 'thorough' with results that are 'convincing.'

results.result: Hundreds of context-specific mutations can directly switch specificity from ERE to SRE, with epistatic effects being necessary in every case and sufficient in almost half. Without epistasis, specificity-switching mutations are reduced by >80%.
results.evaluation: These findings are accepted as part of the core conclusion that epistasis facilitates functional evolution. Reviewers describe the evidence supporting the role of epistasis in specificity switching as compelling, with no concerns raised about these specific quantitative results.

results.result: Despite rampant sign epistasis, 99.8% of functional sequences are connected in a single mutually accessible network. Epistasis increases the number of functional nodes, shortens evolutionary paths, increases direct connections between different specificities, and expands the number of evolutionary paths available.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these sequence space network findings as supporting the conclusion that epistasis potentiates evolution. The analyses are described as thorough and the results as convincing, with no methodological or interpretive concerns raised about the network connectivity findings.

results.result: The functionality of both historical ancestral proteins (egKa and GSKV) and present-day steroid receptors depends critically on pairwise epistasis. The historical transition from ERE- to SRE-specificity altered the genetic architecture itself, changing which sites and pairs confer DNA binding, with the final RH sequence having determinants entirely different from the ancestral sequence.
results.evaluation: These findings about historical sequences are accepted without challenge. Reviewers treat the application of the model to ancestral and extant sequences as valid, and the conclusions about epistasis being critical to historical and modern receptor function are not questioned.

results.result: The experimental library contained all 160,000 combinations of 20 amino acids at four sites and was functionally characterized using a FACS-based Sort-seq assay. Categorization into activation classes substantially reduced technical noise, achieving >97% concordance between replicates.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept the experimental design and data quality without concern. One reviewer notes the dataset was 'previously published' and generated by study authors, and the high replicate concordance is not questioned. The use of categorical rather than continuous data is acknowledged as a methodological choice that reduces noise.

results.result: The ordinal regression model contains terms for main effects and epistatic effects up to third order, fits the experimental data well (99.5% accuracy, deviance 0.86), and genetic scores correlate well with independently measured DNA binding affinity (R²=0.75).
results.evaluation: Reviewers describe the model as 'rigorous' with 'major strengths of being reference free and able to account for global nonlinearity.' The model fit statistics are not questioned, and one reviewer explicitly states the method 'will be valuable to the protein evolution community' and 'will also likely be utilized by other groups.'

results.result: The genetic architecture is dense at first and second orders, with every amino acid state participating in a minimum of 60 pairwise interactions. Specific structural features (small-volume amino acids at site 2 with basic residues at site 3 for nonspecific binding; small hydrophobic residues at site 4 for SRE binding) are identified.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept the finding of dense genetic architecture without challenge. The structural rationalizations for specific effects are not questioned, and the density finding is treated as a valid contrast to some prior studies that found sparse architectures.

results.result: The study's findings differ from prior work because it takes a global rather than local view, analyzes all 20 amino acid states rather than binary comparisons, and uses reference-free methods. Prior reference-based methods and failure to account for global nonlinearities caused spurious inference of higher-order epistasis in previous studies.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirm these methodological distinctions as novel and important. One reviewer states the method 'integrates two key features' that are 'not individually novel but integrating them into a single analysis framework is novel.' The explanation for differences from prior work is accepted without challenge.

results.result: The study acknowledges limitations including potential reduced precision from ordinal modeling (though this reduces noise), unknown generality beyond four sites in one protein (though other studies suggest dense architecture is common), and caution needed before extrapolating to multi-locus phenotypes or complex organismal traits.
results.evaluation: These are author-acknowledged limitations that reviewers do not challenge or expand upon. The reviewers accept the scope of the findings as stated, with one noting the work has 'important implications' for the fields mentioned without disputing the authors' caveats about generalization.

comparisons.comparison: Perfect alignment on experimental design and data quality (C26-C30). Both evaluations accept the library design, methodology, and quality metrics without concern. OpenEval emphasizes quantitative validation while peer reviewers note the dataset was previously published and accept the categorical data approach.

Complete agreement on model structure and validation (C31-C35). Both evaluations strongly support the model's rigor and predictive accuracy. Peer reviewers explicitly praise the reference-free approach and predict the method will be valuable to the community, aligning with OpenEval's positive assessment of model validity.

Strong alignment on genetic architecture findings (C4-C5, C36-C37, C40-C42). Both evaluations support the dominance of low-order effects. OpenEval adds cautionary notes about interpreting higher-order epistasis and methodological limitations (ordinal model precision), while peer reviewers describe findings as 'well-supported' and 'convincing' without raising these concerns. Peer review also addresses C79 (comparison to prior work) not emphasized in OpenEval R3.

Both address structural interpretations (C44-C45) and dense architecture (C43, C81). OpenEval appropriately notes these are post-hoc rationalizations rather than predictions. Peer reviewers accept the structural explanations and density findings without challenge, treating them as valid contrasts to prior sparse architecture studies.

Strong concordance on epistasis enhancing function (C46-C52, C83, C86). Both evaluations recognize this as a major, impactful finding that challenges prevailing views. Peer reviewers explicitly note the conclusion is 'impactful because many previous studies have shown that epistasis constrains evolution,' directly aligning with OpenEval's assessment that this challenges prevailing views.

Perfect alignment on mutational landscape characterization (C53-C59). Both evaluations support the findings on functional transitions, epistatic contributions, and universal sign epistasis. OpenEval adds a caveat about interpreting small-effect mutations, while peer reviewers describe analyses as 'thorough' and 'convincing' without raising concerns.

Complete agreement on epistasis's role in functional evolution (C60-C63). Both evaluations strongly support the specificity-switching findings and necessity/sufficiency analysis. OpenEval emphasizes the direct demonstration through model comparison, while peer reviewers describe evidence as 'compelling' without methodological concerns.

Full concordance on network analysis demonstrating epistasis facilitates evolution (C64-C70). Both evaluations accept the evolutionary simulations and network metrics. OpenEval raises a caveat about assuming equal accessibility of functional variants, which peer reviewers do not address, accepting the facilitating role without this qualification.

Perfect alignment on historical evolution findings (C71-C76). Both evaluations support the conclusions about ancestral sequences requiring epistasis and genetic architecture changing over evolution. OpenEval notes dependencies on ancestral reconstruction accuracy, while peer reviewers accept the application to historical sequences without challenge.

Strong agreement on methodological distinctions from prior work (C77-C78, C80, C82, C84-C85). Both evaluations accept the explanations for differences. Peer reviewers explicitly affirm the novelty of integrating reference-free and global nonlinearity approaches, while OpenEval notes the explanations are plausible but somewhat speculative. Peer review also addresses C81 separately in R10.

Both address the main conceptual contribution about epistasis facilitating evolution (C83-C86). OpenEval provides detailed assessment of how prior work is characterized and notes context-dependency of conclusions. Peer reviewers treat this as a fundamental, well-supported finding without the caveats about generalization that OpenEval mentions.

Perfect alignment on limitations and implications (C87-C93). Both evaluations accept the author-acknowledged limitations without challenge or expansion. OpenEval describes the acknowledgments as 'appropriate' and 'important,' while peer reviewers accept the scope as stated without disputing the caveats about generalization.

Partial overlap on genetic architecture. OpenEval R3 addresses C38-C39 (epistasis and specificity) as part of broader genetic architecture findings, while peer R2 treats these specificity claims as separate, well-supported conclusions about the functional role of pairwise interactions.

OpenEval evaluates characterization of prior work in the field (C2-C3, C10-C17), finding it well-supported with extensive citations. No corresponding peer review evaluation addresses these background claims about limitations in prior approaches.

OpenEval evaluates biological background on steroid hormone receptors and ancestral proteins (C18-C25), finding it well-supported by established knowledge and prior experimental work. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addresses these background claims.

Peer reviewers evaluate specificity claims (C6-C7, C38-C39) as a distinct supported finding about functional roles of pairwise interactions. OpenEval addresses C38-C39 within broader genetic architecture evaluation (R3) but does not separately evaluate C6-C7.
